newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels advance, say capital to fall in days.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels advance, say capital to fall in days.

text.p: Rebel forces in Zaire have announced the capture of a key town that gives them direct access by road and river to the capital Kinshasa.
If confirmed, the fall of Ilebo would be the most important victory by Laurent Kabila's rebels since they seized Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi in Shaba Province two weeks ago.

Rebel "justice minister" Mwenge Kongolo said he believed the fall of Kinshasa was a "matter of days rather than weeks" and added that in his personal opinion there would not be a bloody battle for the capital.

In a separate development, the United States warned the advancing rebels on Wednesday that they could be damaging future relations with Western powers by failing to repatriate Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire.
Washington said reports of mass killings of refugees were "of grave concern".

A senior official of the rebel alliance told a news conference in Lubumbashi that guerrillas had seized three towns east of Kinshasa and were closing in on the last redoubt of President Mobutu Sese Seko's collapsing army.
Of the three, Ilebo is by far the most strategic. An inland port on the Kasai river, it commands direct access to Kinshasa via the Zaire river.
As the terminal of a railway line from Kasai and Shaba provinces, it can assure rebels massive reinforcements by train from Lubumbashi via Kananga, both firmly in rebel hands.

A government spokesman in Kinshasa would neither deny nor confirm the rebel claim. However, a senior official of the SIZARAIL network jointly run by South African, Belgian and Zairean interests said Ilebo had fallen to rebels two days ago.

In the rebel-held territory of the Central African nation, Zairean villagers said Tutsi-dominated rebels slaughtered many Rwandan Hutu refugees at camps south of Kisangani. Aid workers said they had reports up to 55,000 refugees had fled.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Wednesday he was "shocked and appalled by the inhumanity" of Kabila's followers in preventing aid from reaching up to 100,000 refugees.
Most of the refugees are Rwandan Hutus who fled their country after the 1994 massacre of hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu troops and militia.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "If the rebel alliance would like to have normal relations with Western governments, they've got to act in a credible way and a humanitarian way, and that doesn't seem to be the case right here."
Ethnic Tutsis launched Zaire's civil war in October and are still the spearhead of Kabila's rebels, who now control half of the vast country.
Kabila dismissed the reports of a massacre of refugees as "total nonsense".
"There is no truth whatsoever in these reports. The truth is that local Zaireans were attacked by the Rwandan Hutu militia and our army only stepped in to stop the fighting," he told Reuters.
Efforts to end the six-month-old conflict peacefully hit an impasse over the venue of proposed direct talks between Kabila and the embattled Mobutu.
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga Mobutu, said his father was still prepared to meet Kabila but the question remained where.
The president, citing health reasons, wants the talks held in the Congolese capital Brazzaville across the river from Kinshasa, while Kabila has proposed Lubumbashi.
Nzanga said Mobutu declined on health grounds an invitation from President Nelson Mandela to travel to South Africa for the talks. Kabila, in turn, had rejected Brazzaville.
He said Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery last August, was not sick but still convalescing.
